newsitem.title: USA: Oil and wheat prices rise on US North Plains storms.
newsitem.headline: Oil and wheat prices rise on US North Plains storms.

text.p: A powerful spring snowstorm in the U.S. Northern Plains sent oil and wheat prices soaring on Monday, knocking out pumping stations and flooding fields due shortly to be planted with spring crops.

A power outage in Minnesota late Saturday led to the shutdown of three pumping stations, taking out about one million barrels per day of crude oil from IPL Energy Inc's Interprovincial Pipe Line system.

The IPL system, which had been carrying 1.4 million barrels per day, comprises several pipelines that run from western Canada through the U.S. Midwest to Quebec and upstate New York. IPL said it did not believe the pumping stations could be back on line before Wednesday.
Some Canadian producers were expected to have to stop production as their tanks filled to the lids.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for May delivery ended 11 cents a barrel higher at $19.23. May gasoline ended up 0.24 cent at 60.72 cents a gallon, while May heating oil finished 0.02 cent a gallon lower at 53.12 cents.

Monday's price rise in crude was the first in five sessions. Last week, May crude lost almost $1.75 a barrel as views of ample supply driven by increasing imports engulfed the market in a bearish trend.
Wheat prices rose amid growing concern about planting delays in North Dakota, the leading wheat producing state in the United States last year.
"The worries about flooding in the Northern Plains helped wheat," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
Traders said the harsh weather could delay spring wheat seeding by up to two weeks.
"They were ready to go (seeding) west of the Red River Valley and the big weather came in again," one wheat trader said.
Northern Plains states appealed for federal help Monday as storms blocked roads, knocked out power lines and swelled already overflowing rivers, leaving many homeless.

The governors of North and South Dakota both asked President Clinton to declare a federal disaster, and Minnesota was preparing a similar request as the storm brought added misery to what was already shaping up as the flood of the century.

Temperatures also dropped sharply further south in Kansas, where the wheat crop was planted last fall. In the south of the state, where the crop was most advanced and vulnerable, the cold snap was not quite severe enough to do much damage.

"The southern third of the state dodged a bullet. Another three to five degrees and we probably could have seen some damage in that area," said Jim Shroyer, extension wheat agronomist at Kansas State University.
Kansas was the second largest wheat producing state last year, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data.
"It was very cold, but probably not quite cold enough to damage the (Kansas) crop," said Weather Services Corp meteorologist Joel Burgio.
Wheat for May delivery on the Chicago Board of Trade closed 8-3/4 cents higher at $3.80-1/2 a bushel.
Corn prices were also boosted by the flooding as traders speculated the weather would delay corn plantings and force some farmers to switch intended corn acreage to soybeans.
Soybeans can be planted into July in the Midwest, while corn can be sowed only into June.
Corn for May delivery on the CBOT closed 6-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $3.00-3/4.
